newsitem.title: CHINA: China property market stable, housing sales up.
newsitem.headline: China property market stable, housing sales up.

text.p: Property prices in China held mostly steady in the first quarter while residential housing sales started to recover, the China Real Estate Index (CREI) reported on Thursday.

Of the 16 cities surveyed by the CREI office in the first quarter of this year, property price indices of Beijing, Shanghai, the southern boomtown of Shenzhen and the southwestern metropolis of Chongqing rose substantially. Most other cities remained relatively stable.

Beijing's decision to promote Chongqing to a municipality, which took effect in March, pushed the Chongqing property index up 16 points on the CREI index, top among the 16 cities, said Deng Qing, director and chief analyst of the CREI.
In second place was Shenzhen. Its index rose five points amid a boom based on expectations related to neighbouring Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule on July 1, Deng said.
The property market indices for other cities sampled remained relatively stable, with rises or falls of within three points, he said.
Property prices in Shanghai, China's economic hub, fell due to a policy by the city government to reduce the cost of land-use rights to developers and to ease government fees, he said.
China's year-long efforts to stimulate the residential housing market by trimming taxes had pushed housing prices to a new low, fuelling sales, Deng said.

A decision to launch a system of mortgage loans from June would also help the boom in residential housing sales, Meng Xiaosu, president of China National Real Estate Development Group, told reporters.

Xiao Zhuoji, a leading economist from prestigious Beijing University, urged the government to encourage private buying of homes and to lift restrictions on the resale of homes people buy from their work units.

Currently, few Chinese can afford to buy their own home. A policy to allow state work units to sell off housing at discounted prices has failed to result in a market system, due to restrictions on resales intended to prevent profiteering.

Xiao said it was important to spur housing sales to free up large amounts of capital tied up in thousands of unsold apartments as well as to absorb huge amounts of individual savings sitting idle in banks.
By the end of 1996, China had about 50 million square metres of vacant residential housing, occupying about 100 billion yuan ($12 billion) of capital, Xiao said.
China's personal bank savings at end-March reached four trillion yuan and about 300 billion yuan of new capital entered the stock market in 1996, he said.
"So the financial assets of China's urban residents are sufficient to support the development of the real estate sector," he said.
The market for office space was in the doldrums with the CREI index showing a continued nationwide decline in prices, Deng Qing said without elaborating.
"Although the country's property market is developing, we have yet to see any substantial changes," Deng said.
